item.title: Princess Diana's brother Charles Spencer says King Charles 'gaslit' him over memoir claims
item.description: Charles Spencer says he was "gaslit" by King Charles III after Buckingham Palace questioned his memory of a shocking post-Diana conversation.
item.content:encoded:
Princess Diana's brother, Earl Charles Spencer, fired back at Buckingham Palace after the royal household questioned his recollection of a conversation with King Charles III, saying he was being "gaslit" by the monarch.

Earlier this week, The Daily Mail published an excerpt of Spencer's upcoming memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," in which the king's former brother-in-law described having a heated conversation with Charles after Diana's death. In the excerpt, Spencer alleged that Charles said, "We’ll forget her soon enough!," regarding his ex-wife during their exchange.

Buckingham Palace later responded to Spencer's claims, disputing the earl's account of the conversation and suggesting that grief may have affected his memory of events surrounding his sister's death.

KING CHARLES DRAWS ‘LINE IN THE SAND’ WITH PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE AFTER COUPLE CAUGHT OFF GUARD: EXPERT

During an interview with The Mail on Sunday, Spencer took issue with the palace's response.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the king," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said."

"I also thought it was a rather poor imitation of the ‘recollections may vary’ quote, which was a much more elegant way of putting things, but in these circumstances entirely out of place," he added.

The remark referenced the palace's famous "recollections may vary" statement issued after Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's explosive 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey.

In the excerpt, published Wednesday, Spencer described a phone call he said he had with Charles six days after Diana died in August 1997.

"Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting. Then he stopped. I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death," Spencer alleged. "‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’"

PRINCESS DIANA'S HONEYMOON LETTER REVEALS A YOUNG BRIDE 'PLAYING WITH GROWN-UPS' IN THE ROYAL FAMILY

According to the excerpt, the king and the 9th Earl of Spencer disagreed over the decision to have Prince William and Harry, then 15 and 12, walk behind their mother's casket during the funeral procession.

KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson issued a rare statement responding to Spencer's claims.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the statement said, according to People.

Spencer stood by his account of the alleged conversation during an appearance on BBC One's "Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg."

When Kuenssberg pointed out that Buckingham Palace had denied his version of events, Spencer pushed back, saying, "But they haven't actually, Laura. They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they?"

Kuenssberg then read the palace's statement to Spencer, telling him that "the king is plainly furious."

"Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Spencer asked. "Because I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."

Spencer said he remembered the conversation clearly because he had spoken so infrequently with Charles, who was then Prince of Wales.

"I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life," Spencer said. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said."

Spencer said he repeated the alleged comment to close friends and family members immediately afterward "because it was so monstrous."

"Which, Charles, are the public meant to believe?" Kuenssberg asked. "Are they to believe you or are they to believe the king, the head of state of this country who's giving the impression very forcefully that this didn't happen? Who are we to believe?"

"Well, I'm telling the truth," Spencer replied.

"So, the king is giving an impression to the country that's not true. Misleading people, even lying?" Kuenssberg asked.

"I can hardly be responsible for what Buckingham Palace says," Spencer replied. "All I can tell you is what was said and what I heard and what shocked me. What else would have made me hang up on the king that day? It was something as outrageous as that slur against Diana."

When asked whether William and Harry would be upset by his account of the alleged phone call with their father, Spencer suggested his nephews were already familiar with his version of events.

"Well, I don't like to talk about what I've been speaking about to William and Harry, but this will not be a surprise to them," he said. "I will tell you that these words will not be a surprise to them."

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We won’t be offering any comment."

Diana died at age 36 after suffering injuries sustained in a car accident in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris, France. Her partner, Dodi Fayed, and the driver, Henri Paul, also died in the crash.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

At the time of her death, she and Charles had been divorced for about one year. The two married in July 1981, announced their separation in December 1992 and finalized their divorce in August 1996.

Harry wrote about the decision to have him and his brother walk behind their mother's coffin in his 2023 memoir, "Spare," saying that "several adults were aghast" and that "mummy’s brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell," and that he told the royal family, "You can’t make these boys walk behind their mother’s coffin! It’s barbaric."

Spencer previously spoke about his opposition to William and Harry walking behind their mother's coffin. He told BBC Radio 4's "Today" in 2017 that he found the decision "bizarre and cruel."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It was the most horrifying half an hour of my life," he said. "It was just ghastly. And it was far worse than having to deliver a speech at the end of it. It was the worst part of the day by a considerable margin, walking behind, well, my sister’s body, with two boys who were obviously massively grieving their mother.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And it was this sort of bizarre circumstance where we were told you had to look straight ahead," he continued. "But the feeling, the sort of crashing tidal wave of grief coming at you as you went down this sort of tunnel of deep emotion, it was really harrowing actually, and I still have nightmares about it now."

"Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" is set to be released Sept. 22.

Fox News Digital's Lori Bashian contributed to this report.

item.title: 'Lioness' season 3 finale reveals who orchestrated Joe's kidnapping all along
item.description: Reddit reactions poured in after "Lioness" revealed the puppet master behind Joe's kidnapping in a twist rooted in Zoe Saldaña's season one arc.
item.content:encoded:
*WARNING: Spoilers below

"Lioness" season three is officially in the books, and it gave fans a wild surprise at the end.

Season three of Taylor Sheridan's hit CIA/military series focused heavily on the kidnapping of Joe (Zoe Saldaña) and the attempts to rescue her.

LIONESS SEASON 3 EPISODE 7 DELIVERS JOE'S RESCUE IN A GUNFIGHT FANS WON'T STOP TALKING ABOUT

She was eventually rescued in episode seven in a brutally violent and bloody gunfight. That left one major problem unresolved:

Who was the puppet master behind it all?

Fans were led to believe throughout different parts of the season that it could be the Russians, Ukrainians or the Iranians.

The answer was revealed on Sunday.

Something much more complex and rooted in the history of "Lioness."

It was revealed in the final moments that Aaliyah Amrohi, the daughter of the season one target, was the puppet master who orchestrated the entire operation against Joe as revenge for the killing of her father.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S ATTENTION TO WEAPONS HANDLING SETS 'LIONESS' APART FROM OTHER MILITARY DRAMAS

It's also clear that Aaliyah isn't going to stop, and the stage is set for the fourth and likely final season. The season finale – titled "The Unraveling" – also featured an epic restaurant shootout scene when Joe ordered her team to engage the man who kidnapped her. Let's just say things didn't go as planned.

Reactions to the season finale poured in on Reddit. Check out some of the reactions from viewers below:

ZOE SALDAÑA SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES INSTAGRAM POSTS FROM BRUTAL 'LIONESS' TORTURE SCENE

The surprising twist, which I figured out during the interrogation scene, is another example of Sheridan keeping fans on edge and always guessing what's coming next.

It's actually a bit surprising he managed to keep such a large reveal hidden from the public. It came shockingly close to slipping out, judging from a random Reddit post.

A woman shared a photo of herself with Stephanie Nur, the actress who plays Aaliyah, taken when the show was filming in Fort Worth after seeing her at a coffee shop.

It certainly feels like the next season will be the conclusion of the show, and seeing as how so much of Cruz and Joe's arcs are tied back to the actions of season one, it makes perfect sense. While I have no idea what's coming, my guess is many characters won't make it out alive. It wouldn't make any sense if they had happy endings.

It goes against everything the show has given fans through three seasons.

item.title: GOP fiscal hawk sounds alarm on 'out of control' federal spending, saying 'both parties have failed us'
item.description: Sen. Paul, who said "both parties have failed us," does not support President Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to American adults if the GOP wins both chambers in the midterms.
item.content:encoded:
With the U.S. national debt soaring above $40 trillion and the federal government engaging in massive deficit spending, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. — a fiscal hawk who says the situation is "out of control" and "both parties have failed us" — does not support President Donald Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress during the midterms.

The president floated the idea during a speech earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, calling it "the Trump dividend."

Asked about the president's proposal during an interview on Thursday, Paul told Fox News Digital that he is not in favor of giving away "dividends when there's a deficit."

"We're running $2 trillion dollars short," he said, noting that he "can't imagine giving out money when you're running a deficit."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Friday.

RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS

America's soaring national debt has surpassed the staggering sum of $40 trillion and shows no signs of stopping.

"And so, the debt is very important. So it's not just important that it might bankrupt us or overwhelm us in some kinda crisis in the future," Paul said, acknowledging that as "a possibility. But every day you're being hurt by it because it's stealing the value" of people's earnings, he indicated.

"So it is literally out of control," Paul said. "And really both parties have failed us because both parties are afraid to tell the American public that some things they like from government would have to be reduced when we cut costs."

Paul has a plan that he says would balance the budget through a series of spending cuts over five years.

GOP LAWMAKERS PUMP BRAKES ON TRUMP'S $5K CHECK PROMISE: 'WHERE ARE YOU GETTING THE MONEY?'

"Now when I first introduced it, it was a 1% cut, or a one-penny plan, and you cut spending 1% a year for five years, and with economic growth increasing revenue, the lines cross at about five years," balancing the budget, he explained. "Well, when COVID came along, both parties frankly started passin' out money like drunken sailors and... the deficit ballooned. Now to balance the budget in five years it's called the six-penny plan cuz it takes about a 6% cut. But it still shows you that we wouldn't have to eliminate everything."

While the cuts under his proposal would not apply to Social Security, they would apply to Medicare, he indicated, though he suggested it could be possible "to cut Medicare 6% without cutting any health benefits," saying that he thinks there is a lot of "waste and fraud in" the program. He also suggested that additional means testing could be used to achieve the Medicare spending cuts.

Paul — who ran for president in 2016 but dropped out after placing fifth in the Iowa GOP presidential caucuses — is considering throwing his hat into the ring again.

"I'd say we're 50-50," he said. "I do think that there should be a candidate on the Republican side, at least, who believes that international trade is good for our country and good for the economy, that believes in free markets, that isn't a big believer in big government coming in and managing contracts and owning parts of countries, that isn't a believer in giving out money we don't have."

RAND PAUL SAYS HE'S '50-50' ON RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028, 'THINKING ABOUT IT'

Paul said he does not "want there to be a choice of four populists running for president," noting that he wants there to be "at least one free-market candidate. I could be that, or maybe somebody else could be," he said, indicating that he will decide after the midterm elections.

item.title: CHAD WOLF: Congress has a chance to stop China from turning your car into a Chinese spy
item.description: The Connected Vehicle Security Act aims to shield the United States from Chinese espionage via batteries, sensors and software in modern cars.
item.content:encoded:
Recent reporting about a British naval drone unknowingly sending data to China offers an urgent warning to policymakers in the United States.

During a routine cybersecurity assessment, the U.K. Ministry of Defence exposed a serious breach. It found that a component in its naval drones was secretly transmitting data to China. The drone was British. The hidden vulnerability was not.

CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'

To be clear, this is part of Beijing’s playbook. It uses intellectual-property theft, cyberespionage and industrial policy to become indispensable to Western supply chains and then exploits that access to collect intelligence and create vulnerabilities it can use against its adversaries.

Our standard response has been to restrict Chinese technology only after the risks become impossible to ignore, often spending billions of dollars to rip and replace equipment already embedded in American networks and infrastructure.

CHINESE ESPIONAGE STEALS $600 BILLION FROM US FIRMS YEARLY. IT’S TIME FOR GOVERNMENT TO ACT

Now, Beijing has its sights on conducting widespread espionage and sabotage in another sector – automobiles. But this time, America has the opportunity to act before it’s too late.

China is now the world’s largest vehicle exporter, and Chinese companies are major players not only in electric vehicles but in the batteries, software, sensors and connected technologies critical to modern cars.

Chinese automakers are using a variety of strategies to enter U.S. markets, and China’s rise as an automotive power presents an obvious challenge for American manufacturers. But as cars become more connected, China’s entry poses severe national security risks.

Modern vehicles are computers on wheels, equipped with cameras, microphones, sensors, GPS systems and internet-connected hardware. They collect enormous amounts of data about their drivers and surroundings, while software increasingly controls critical functions including steering, braking and acceleration.

KARR BLUETOOTH FLAW EXPOSES 2.2M CARS TO THEFT RISK

In the wrong hands, that access could provide a powerful tool for surveillance and espionage or potentially allow an adversary to remotely manipulate or disable vehicles.

Chinese cars on American roads would represent the most direct threat. But Chinese companies don’t need to sell millions of vehicles in America to gain a foothold in the U.S. automotive ecosystem.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

The same risks can be embedded in American, European, Japanese or South Korean vehicles through Chinese-made batteries, software and connected components.

At scale, these technologies could offer Beijing an extraordinary intelligence picture: where Americans live and work, which roads they travel and which vehicles regularly enter military bases, ports, power plants and other sensitive facilities.

In a crisis or conflict, the consequences could extend beyond surveillance. Vulnerabilities in technology embedded across millions of vehicles could potentially provide an adversary a means to disrupt transportation on a massive societal scale.

Congress has an opportunity to address that threat before it manifests by passing the bipartisan Connected Vehicle Security Act, sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno and Michigan Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin. The legislation builds on the Commerce Department’s connected-vehicle rule, which restricts vehicles, software and connectivity hardware linked to our enemies.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Commerce concluded that foreign-adversary access to these technologies could enable the collection of sensitive data and remote manipulation of vehicles.

That was an important first step, but we must do more. Executive rulemaking can be reversed, but Congress has the chance to make it last. Only an act of Congress can make these national security protections permanent.

CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

The Connected Vehicle Security Act would codify and expand the protections outlined in the Commerce Department’s rulemaking across the supply chain. Critically, it reaches beyond finished Chinese automobiles to the connected technologies inside them, including software, communications equipment and electronics integrated into batteries.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The Senate Commerce Committee advanced it unanimously in July. Congress should pass this legislation and send it to the president’s desk.

America has repeatedly become dependent on Chinese technology only to later discover how difficult and expensive those dependencies were to unwind. Connected vehicles offer a chance to act before another dependency becomes entrenched.

item.title: NASCAR wives make explosive claims after husbands brawl at Bristol & driver launches water bottle into scrum
item.description: Ryan Blaney hunted down Carson Hocevar after a Bristol wreck, sparking NASCAR's wildest fight as Gianna Blaney posted explosive claims online.
item.content:encoded:
Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

You see? THIS is why I've always been baffled by NASCAR's decision to move the Bristol night race to September.

We had, easily, the most viral moment of the racing season Saturday night, and it went directly against Ole Miss-LSU. Chase Elliott said it many years ago, and it's still true today ...

STOP COMPETING WITH FOOTBALL.

Phew. OK. I needed to get that off my chest before we dive into the biggest fight this sport has seen since Allison-Yarborough.

NASCAR'S MOST POPULAR DRIVER HAS A TIKTOK GIRLFRIEND THAT'S CAUSING A STIR, AND HE DOESN'T CARE

Fine. That's probably an overreaction. But hey! This Ryan Blaney-Carson Hocevar scrum still a good one!

For Carson, at least. Not sure Blaney got a ton of licks in, but Lordy, he is scrappy. We'll get into it today, obviously. What else are we gonna talk about? Joey Logano winning?

Joey Logano won! There. Happy? Moving on ...

I've also got Blaney's wife, former Hooters girl Gianna Tulio (Blaney), posting some explosive accusations on Instagram about Carson, another NASCAR wife chiming in, NASCAR itself seemingly not doing anything about it, and Ty Gibbs launching a water bottle into the scene of the crime.

That, by the way, may have been the funniest part of the whole thing. You'll see.

Four tires, a couple splashes of that Sunoco racin' fuel, and maybe a raw steak for Blaney's left eye ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'She Said WHAT?' edition — is LIVE!

No reason to wait around today ... we've had two days to marinate on it. You've all seen the fight by now. We've all seen it.

I know folks despise him, but very few people can make NASCAR trend on X during a college football Saturday night. Carson Hocevar did just that.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

NASCAR needs a villain, and has NEEDED a villain for the longest time. They have one in Carson Hocevar.

Let's dive in:

Goodness gracious. What a fight. What a scene.

Couple things ...

Amazing. What's he doing!? No clue. Everyone just hates Hocevar so much, they all wanted a little piece of the action.

Side note: Gibbs finished fifth in Kyle Busch's M&M's paint scheme Saturday night and led 120 laps. Well done, Ty.

Anyway, here's Hocevar after what he called the first fight of his life:

"That's the first time I've ever hit anybody," Hocevar said. "It's a cool story at least, to be at Bristol of all places. "I don't know what a decent one (punch) feels like. I've never thrown one."

Hocevar went on to talk about the crash that started all of this, saying he didn't intend to wreck Blaney (duh), and that perhaps the driver of the No. 12 Penske Ford wrecked himself.

Again, I don't want to pick sides here, but ... I think I might be with Carson on this one:

Man, that's a tough one. Hocevar said he was on the brakes pretty hard. I'm not sure I buy that, but I also don't know that he needed to be. It's Bristol. You just made a crossover move, and you have the line.

To me, Blaney went low to try and block the run, and Hocevar's nose was already there. That's just how I see it. I don't think there was any intent.

It didn't matter, though. This was the last straw for Carson. Two weeks ago it was Brad Keselowski, and Saturday night it was Ryan Blaney.

Hocevar, by the way, told me after Daytona that he didn't expect to have any enemies on the track during this 10-race Chase. He said that with a straight face.

Didn't take long!

Those enemies, by the way, ain't just on the track, either:

"Not surprised by #77 aggressive behavior with the criminal record he has," Blaney's wife, Gianna, said in response to NASCAR's Instagram video of the fight. "Wait I forgot most of you don't know about it because he got it paid off!! Oops *allegedly*."

Well ... that's certainly a statement to make!

Gianna, by the way, hasn't deleted those comments, which — again — were in response to an official post from NASCAR. So, yes, NASCAR has certainly seem them, and they aren't making her take them down.

It's interesting, to say the least.

By the way, Gianna wasn't the only one feeling it after Bristol. McCall Gaulding, the wife of Zane Smith, chimed in as well:

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Just trying to make his fans aware on who they support," she said under her own post. When a fan pressed her for more info, Gaulding claimed "we've tried and it gets covered up."

item.title: Shocking discovery of ancient bones turns couple's kitchen renovation into 'crime scene'
item.description: A homeowner's kitchen renovation turned into a spooky police investigation after a builder unearthed Anglo-Saxon human bones roughly 1,000 years old.
item.content:encoded:
Ancient human remains that turned a couple's home renovation into a crime investigation have finally been laid to rest — with the homeowner recently speaking out about the ordeal.

Ross Sledger, 49, was at work in spring 2019 when a builder working on a kitchen addition at his home unearthed what appeared to be human bones, news agency SWNS reported.

The remains were formally re-interred this August during a ceremony at a church near Sledger's home in Wye, Kent, in southeastern England.

ANCIENT 'SEATED' SKELETONS UNEARTHED BENEATH MODERN SCHOOL SITE, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS

Sledger said he initially thought little of the discovery, assuming the bones belonged to a farm animal or pet, SWNS reported. 

"[The builder] said, 'I’ve found some bones,' and I said, 'Great,' thinking it was farming or pets," Sledger said.

Sledger said he was stunned to learn the remains could be human.

"As you can imagine, a lot of language came out of my mouth. I was thinking, 'You must be joking, this is a wind-up,' but he said, 'I’m deadly serious,'" Sledger recalled. 

AIRBNB GUESTS CHECK INTO THEIR RENTAL TO FIND STARTLING DISCOVERY ON WALL

The bones, later determined to be Anglo-Saxon remains roughly 1,000 years old, caused a stir — and a police investigation.

Around 10 officers went to the home to sift through the backyard, with investigators eventually finding remains of a second body.

In all, the grisly discovery included a femur, two skulls, ribs, part of a pelvis and fragments of a humerus and finger bones.

"They thought it was a crime scene," Sledger said. "They had to have an officer overnight, and every half hour he had to get out of his car."

SISTERS IN VIRAL VIDEO REVEAL TRUTH IN ‘EERIE’ FAMILY PHOTO THEY DISCOVERED AT RENTAL HOME

"That set off the neighbor's floodlights, which set off my dog barking. So as you can imagine, I didn’t get much sleep that night," he added, as SWNS noted.

About 48 hours after the initial discovery, specialists confirmed the remains were ancient and not related to a modern-day crime.

But the discoveries didn't end there. 

Sledger later uncovered what he described as "knuckles and fingers" while installing artificial grass in his backyard — which caused some renovation-related anxiety.

"I was thinking, 'Oh no, this is going to delay it. I’ve got bricklayers next week,'" Sledger said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I was thinking, 'This could take months,' but luckily, they were done and dusted by the end of the weekend, which was good."

After the police investigation ended, Sledger said the remains were transferred to a historical society and eventually to a local vicar, though arranging their final resting place took time.

"I think it was a question of getting permission and whether they would be allowed to be there," Sledger added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"I think it was a bit more red tape than anything else."

At the August re-interment ceremony, the vicar chose the hymn "Jerusalem," which Sledger said offered a fitting tribute to the ancient remains.

Sledger's backyard isn't the only one in the United Kingdom to yield an unexpected piece of history.

Another British couple made a historically valuable — though far less grim — discovery in their own backyard recently. 

The Hampshire couple uncovered a hoard of 70 historic English coins while adjusting a fence near a flower bed in 2020.

New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough continued to show massive improvement from Year 1 to Year 2 as he led the team to a 24-17 victory over the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday.

Shough scored the go-ahead touchdown from the 1-yard line and New Orleans’ defense locked down Baltimore’s offense to seal the win in the closing moments. But, as with most NFL games, the officiating came under fire over Shough’s touchdown.

The NFL world wondered how Shough’s play was ruled a touchdown.

An NFL executive defended the ruling.

The Saints bounced back from a close loss last week against the Detroit Lions.

item.title: Tourists seeking 'dramatic' photo on isolated beach trapped by incoming tide
item.description: Drone footage captures three tourists spelling out "SOS" on Oregon's Lost Boy Beach after a rising tide trapped them in the Tillamook County cove.
item.content:encoded:
Tourists went to snap an iconic photo on Oregon's Lost Boy Beach and wound up getting one taken of themselves in a storybook SOS rescue by the local fire department last week.

Three unnamed sea gawkers were stranded for five hours Wednesday, Sept. 16, after a rising tide cut them off from the mainland at the secluded Tillamook County cove. Having reportedly lost cell phone service at the bottom of the steep cliff, the group managed to contact 911 using an emergence satellite feature, The Oregonian reported.

Netarts-Oceanside Fire District received the call and found them stranded on the shrinking patch of beach with the tide rolling in on them, using a drone to capture footage of them spelling out a large "SOS" with sticks.

11 VISITORS TRAPPED AS DANGEROUS FLASH FLOODING TEARS THROUGH ICONIC NATIONAL PARK

Lost Boy Beach is accessible only by scrambling over rocky terrain and passing through a sea cave that is open at both ends. While the small beach is inviting during low tide, the rising water blocks the only exit.

"When people are stranded there, we may not be able to get to them," NOFD Chief Jeff McBrayer told the paper.

HELICOPTER RESCUE CREW CAUGHT ON CAMERA SAVING 2 CLIMBERS TRAPPED ALONG POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH CLIFF

Crews initially considered waiting for the tide to recede, but opted for an active rescue due to rough surf, the presence of sneaker waves, and the fact that the tourists were already wet and cold, he added.

Navigating the dangerous conditions, rescuers hugged the remaining shoreline while secured to ropes instead of wading directly through the unpredictable water. Once they reached the tourists, responders provided life vests, clipped the group to the safety ropes, and guided them through the surf to a secure area where they could walk out on their own.

CALIFORNIA DAD PARALYZED FROM NECK DOWN AFTER DIVING INTO OCEAN TO RESCUE CHILD

The visitors emerged from the ordeal with only minor bumps and bruises.

Following the rescue, Chief McBrayer used the incident to remind coastal visitors of the area's deceptive dangers of exploring isolated coves.

"You have to ask a local or check a tide app on a phone for tide information," he said.

HIKERS STRANDED ON MOUNT SHASTA AFTER RELYING ON AI TO PLAN TRIP, SHERIFF SAYS

Lost Boy Beach, situated on the northern Oregon coast just south of a towering basalt cliff, derives its ominous name from a century-old local legend. According to regional lore, the highly secluded spot was named after a young boy who was believed to have drowned after being trapped by the incoming tide. While it remains unverified if the tragic tale is historically accurate, the name has persisted for roughly 100 years, functioning as a built-in, enduring warning to visitors about the cove's unpredictable and deadly conditions.

Historically, reaching this hidden stretch of sand has remained notoriously treacherous, wedged between Short Beach to the north and Tunnel Beach — sometimes known as Star Trek Beach — to the south. Unlike its neighboring Short Beach, which finally received a community-built "stairway of 100 steps" around 2000 to stop visitors from cracking their heads on a slippery cliff face, Lost Boy Beach has never featured safe overland access.

Navigating to the beach from either side is exceptionally dangerous, with access only vaguely possible during rare, extreme low-tide events that occur just a couple of times a year.

item.title: If Trump wants to lower drug prices, his obvious free-riding targets are outside the US
item.description: President Donald Trump secured nine drug pricing deals, but lasting relief requires pressuring foreign countries to pay their fair share for medicine.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump just secured nine new pricing agreements with drug manufacturers that could help reduce what Americans pay for many prescription medicines.

The deals demonstrate Trump's commitment to lowering drug prices for patients. The president's dedication – and his desire to negotiate with companies individually, rather than imposing broad mandates – is commendable. But his efforts would be better directed at the root cause of high drug prices: foreign countries free-riding on American drug innovation.

To deliver lasting price reductions while protecting U.S. leadership in biomedical innovation, the Trump administration must focus its negotiating strategy overseas – and intensify its push to make other countries pay their fair share for the medicines America develops.

TRUMP EXPANDS TRUMPRX PRESCRIPTION DRUG DISCOUNT PROGRAM TO MORE THAN 800 MEDICATIONS

For decades, wealthy foreign governments have used price controls, mandatory rebates, reimbursement delays and other policies to suppress what they pay for innovative medicines. These measures allow foreign countries to reap the benefits of new treatments while forcing Americans to bear a disproportionate share of the cost of developing them.

American patients currently account for roughly three-quarters of pharmaceutical profits and over half of global research and development spending – far more than America's share of the world economy.

If U.S. leaders want to correct this imbalance, putting more pressure on drugmakers isn't the solution. Instead, the administration must focus on getting other countries to end their free-riding practices.

Forcing U.S. prices lower without increasing foreign countries' contributions risks harming both American patients and our broader biotech industry. Some members of Congress, for example, have proposed writing "most-favored-nation" drug pricing into law – permanently tying U.S. drug prices to the artificially low prices paid abroad.

ROBERT F KENNEDY JR: THE FUTURE OF MEDICINE SHOULD BE BUILT IN AMERICA

Such an approach would effectively import foreign price controls into America – reducing funding for future research and development and slowing the development of new treatments. It could also threaten jobs, undermine manufacturing investment and weaken U.S. drugmakers' ability to compete with China.

To sustain both lower prices and continued innovation here at home, other wealthy countries will need to step up and shoulder more of the costs.

3 STEPS THAT COULD STOP FRAUD AND MAKE HEALTHCARE MORE AFFORDABLE FOR ALL AMERICANS

Fortunately, the Trump administration's negotiating skills offer a way to make that happen. The same hard-charging approach it has used to negotiate recent deals with manufacturers can also be applied abroad to pressure foreign governments to reform their pricing policies.

The United Kingdom is a clear example. Last year, Trump negotiated a deal that will require Britain to increase what it pays for new medicines by 25%. As Britain contributes more toward developing new medicines, the cost burden on the United States will decrease.

MARK CUBAN SHOOTS DOWN PRESIDENTIAL BID AS HE TEAMS UP WITH TRUMP ADMIN TO CUT HEALTHCARE COSTS

The administration is also laying the groundwork for a similar agreement with Germany. In June, it launched a formal investigation into how Germany's drug price controls have harmed American commerce. This investigation will give American trade officials the leverage they need to negotiate fairer pricing policies and practices with German policymakers.

The next step should be to apply this strategy to other wealthy nations. Countries like Japan, France and Switzerland use tactics similar to Germany's to pay far less than fair value for new drugs. In Japan, for example, roughly half of newly launched medicines are subject to annual price cuts.

INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE

According to one analysis, if other developed countries all paid U.S. prices for new prescription drugs, global pharmaceutical revenue would rise by more than $254 billion. That would provide a major influx of revenue for American drug innovators – potentially fueling a research and development boom that would create jobs across the country while delivering more and cheaper lifesaving treatments for patients.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Trump has shown he's committed to bringing drug prices down – and that his administration has the negotiating skill and leverage needed to extract real concessions from foreign freeloaders.

By refocusing its negotiating efforts on America's trading partners and pushing them to pay their fair share for pharmaceutical innovation, the Trump administration can help lower prices for American patients while preserving U.S. biopharma leadership.

item.title: Fitness expert reveals 6 things people over 35 should do after workouts to stay strong
item.description: Fitness coach Jacob Zemer shares six post-workout recovery strategies for adults over 35, from sleep and heat therapy to protein and stretching tips.
item.content:encoded:
The most important part of a workout may happen after it ends.

As adults age, muscles can become less responsive to protein and other muscle-building signals, making post-exercise recovery critical for repairing tissue and preserving strength.

Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach, focuses heavily on recovery with his clients, who primarily range from 35 to 55 years old.

ONE MUSCLE PROTEIN MAY HOLD THE KEY TO STAYING STRONGER AS YOU AGE, STUDY FINDS

"Most of my clients are really focused on longevity," he told Fox News Digital. "They're not people who are looking to be bodybuilders or power lifters – they want to age well."

Zemer shared the following six ways adults over 35 can recover more effectively after exercise.

"Getting seven to nine hours of quality sleep is vital," Zemer told Fox News Digital.

COMMON BEDROOM MISTAKE COULD BE QUIETLY TAKING A TOLL ON YOUR HEALTH, EXPERTS SAY

He suggested the following steps to support deeper, more restorative sleep.

Getting regular checkups and completing recommended lab work can also help identify issues that may interfere with recovery, according to Zemer.

"Make sure you’re keeping up with what's going on with your hormones," he advised. "Make sure everything in your body is functioning properly, because as we age, our bodies change."

3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS

Experts emphasize, however, that preventive testing should be personalized based on factors such as age, gender, symptoms and medical history.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for conditions including high blood pressure, prediabetes/type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis.

Heat exposure may be another way to support muscle strength and recovery after exercise, Zemer suggested.

Warmth causes blood vessels to widen, increasing circulation to tired muscles and potentially helping to deliver nutrients involved in repair.

A 2025 review of 22 studies found that nearly half of participants reported improved muscle-function recovery with heat therapy.

"If you don't have access to a sauna, taking a hot shower after your workout releases heat proteins that may help with recovery – and actually it helps improve what we call ‘gains’ from the gym," the trainer told Fox News Digital.

"After you get done working out, your muscles are shortened," Zemer said. "And so you want to re-lengthen them by stretching."

As strength training can put significant wear and tear on the body, it’s important to maintain full mobility by moving through a complete range of motion and stretching afterward, according to the expert.

Getting adequate protein after a workout to aid in muscle repair and rebuilding, Zemer emphasized.

The International Society of Sports Nutrition recommends targeting about 20 to 40 grams of high-quality protein after training. For active adults, the general guideline is roughly 1.4 to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Protein needs should be individualized, however, particularly for people with certain medical conditions.

Hydration is also important prior to working out, Zemer added.

"If you don't drink enough water, you're really setting yourself up for failure when you're in the session, which is going to cause you to have lackluster results," he said.

"You just did something that, even if it’s healthy and has a positive impact on your body, still stresses your body," Zemer said.

"Your cortisol’s high. So getting a good meal and a little bit of rest before you move on with your day" can help the body recover.

The goal is to give the nervous system and muscles the resources they need to recover.

A 2026 review described exercise as a cycle of "stress response, adaptation and recovery," noting that the benefits of workouts depend on sufficient recovery time, sleep and energy availability.

While it’s normal and generally a good thing to feel sore after exercise, Zemer said there’s a fine line between "good" and "bad" soreness.

"The soreness should be only for a short period of time, like maybe a day or so after you're done training," he told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"If it takes you a full week to recover, you simply trained too hard."

Zemer noted that the body adapts to training gradually, so people should ease into a new fitness routine rather than pushing too hard too soon.

"If you have extended amounts of soreness that exceed two or three days, you did too much," he said. "If your knees and joints ache, you did too much."

That doesn’t mean it’s necessary to stop working out, however.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"It just means maybe drop back what you did by 30% and start from there," Zemer advised. "For example, if you did six sets of legs, try instead to do four sets of legs the next time you train. That's going to make it far more effective for your recovery."

The most important thing to recognize, according to the trainer, is that exercise-induced endorphins can temporarily mask pain. Discomfort that seems manageable during a workout may feel worse later, once those chemicals wear off.

"If something hurts in the gym when you have your endorphins going strong, it's going to hurt really bad later – and that's the last thing you want, because if you're hurt, you're not going to be able to train consistently."

item.title: NFL's dumbest moment of Week 2 goes to Jets coach Aaron Glenn who played not to lose at end of regulation
item.description: Sometimes the dumbest NFL play is a coaching decision. Aaron Glenn admitted he never considered a timeout that could have saved the Jets' game.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, the dumbest play of the week in the NFL is not actually a play at all but a play-call or decision by a coach. We're looking at you, Aaron Glenn.

The New York Jets coach, in his second season with the Jets making all the decisions, has been a study in inconsistency with his clock management.

And he was downright worthy of hard questioning on Sunday after a 20-17 overtime loss to the Green Bay Packers – because maybe this game didn't need to go to overtime at all.

STEFON DIGGS GUILTY OF NFL'S DUMBEST MOVE OF WEEK 1 AND IT MAY HAVE DECIDED COMMANDERS LOSS TO EAGLES

But Glenn curiously decided it would.

In the fourth quarter, you see, the Packers had the ball and the Jets limited them to a 5-yard completion on third-and-10. So the Packers faced a fourth-down play with about 50 seconds left to play.

Glenn could have immediately called time out.

He could have immediately forced the Packers to punt on fourth down from midfield and given his offense one final opportunity in regulation to perhaps run three or four plays, get in field goal range, and pull out a win.

Glenn had timeouts. But he didn't use them. He apparently didn't even think of using them.

"I didn't," Glenn admitted after the game. "I didn't consider using that. I know exactly what you're talking about. No, I didn't think of using the timeout at that point at all."

Fair enough. If we're giving Glenn the benefit of the doubt, we have to believe he probably thought it all through and made an informed decision.

But informed decisions come with reasoning. So what was Glenn's reasoning for not using time-outs that would have given his offense a chance?

"Man, I want to go back and really look at it, you know, to be honest with you," Glenn said. "I think they were in a situation where they were trying a no-brainer, and they took the no-brainer, or they took the penalty on that."

The Packers did indeed praise Jesus that Glenn didn't call time out, so they did the no-brainer thing and sat on the ball and took a delay of game penalty. The 10-second runoff on the penalty left only two seconds on the clock.

And the Packers, intent on launching a Hail Mary on fourth down, suffered a Jordan Love sack instead, to end regulation.

But, again, if Glenn had called that timeout immediately after the third-down play, the Jets might have had maybe those 50 seconds to force Green Bay to punt and give their offense a chance.

"Yeah, and if they would have punted it, that would put us in a backed-up situation," Glenn argued. "They could have punted the ball and put us in a backed-up situation right there. So that was the reason why."

This is not the way.

If Glenn had forced the issue, he actually has no clue what might have happened next. The punter might have dropped the snap. The punt might have gotten blocked. His punt returner, challenged as he's been with holding on to the ball, might have contributed a dynamic return.

But instead, Glenn made certain his offense would have no final opportunity to win the game in regulation.

New York Jets fans and the media covering the team, being the understanding and patient people they are, obviously excused Glenn's strategy.

No, wait—no, they didn't.

"This debacle falls on Aaron Glenn," the attention-grabbing part of a New York Post headline blared.

Fans also took to social media and roasted Glenn.

item.title: NFL Week 2 Sunday takeaways: Packers are Jekyll and Hyde, Bengals have a defense, Chargers' season is over
item.description: From the Packers' comeback win over the Jets to Caleb Williams' injury scare, every NFL Week 2 Sunday game delivered surprising takeaways.
item.content:encoded:
One week of NFL football gives fans and the media something to talk about. Two weeks gives them just enough information to start believing that they might actually know something (they still don't, and that includes me).

Week 2 offered the first chance to see which opening-week performances were meaningful and which were complete mirages. Although, thanks to confirmation bias, nothing that happened probably changed anyone's opinion (including mine).

Below, you will find my biggest takeaway from each game on the Week 2 Sunday slate.

Takeaway: Don't sleep on the Panthers offense.

Carolina gave up 59 points to Chicago in Week 1, which overshadowed a solid offensive performance of their own. The Panthers scored 37 points and gained 478 yards of offense against the Bears. Of course, the defensive no-show made it all for naught. But after another 30+ point performance, suddenly it looks like Bryce Young's step forward in 2025 wasn't a fluke and he might be taking another step in 2026.

ATLANTA FALCONS ARE DEALING WITH THE WORST QUARTERBACK SITUATION IN THE NFL AND IT ISN'T EVEN CLOSE

Takeaway: The Saints are a really fun team to watch.

Last week, New Orleans nearly pulled off a massive upset of the Detroit Lions but fell just short. This week, they didn't let the opportunity slip away. More importantly, at least for general NFL fans, this team is fun. Tyler Shough, coming off a fan-voted Rookie of the Year season, doesn't look like a one-hit wonder. If Chris Olave can stay healthy, Saints-Panthers might be must-watch TV and that's not something I ever thought I'd type.

Takeaway: What a difference a week makes.

A week ago, pundits were declaring that the 2026 Chicago Bears offense might be one of the greatest of all time. That was.. premature. Now, there's nothing more important than the health of quarterback Caleb Williams, who was carted off the field in the fourth quarter with a hamstring injury. But Chicago didn't look great even when Williams was in the game. Weather was a factor, of course, but the two teams that scored 98 points combined in Week 1 only mustered 12 in Week 2.

Takeaway: If the Bengals can win games like this, the rest of the NFL is in trouble.

In the Joe Burrow era, the Bengals have basically relied on their star quarterback to help them outscore opponents. This game was the opposite. In fact, Houston outgained Cincinnati by over 100 yards and had 10 more first downs. But the Bengals defense kept clamping down, forcing four turnovers on downs and only allowing two field goals. If Cincinnati's defense can almost singlehandedly win games, the Bengals are one of the best teams in the league.

Takeaway: The Steelers are not a fun team to watch.

Right now, Pittsburgh is like the anti-New Orleans. While the Saints have a young quarterback and a young receiver helping them move the ball up and down the field, the Steelers have an old quarterback whose career probably should have ended three years ago and an overpaid veteran receiver who can't catch anything. That's not a fun combination.

Takeaway: I honestly don't know what to even think about this game.

I was ready to declare that the Jets might actually be good, then they blew a 10-point fourth-quarter lead to the Packers and I'm back on the "oh wait, they're still the Jets" train. Similarly, what even are the Packers? They had a huge lead last week against the Vikings, blew it, and looked dead in the water for three quarters against the Jets. I guess they're just this year's ultimate Jekyll and Hyde team. They look fantastic at times and utterly terrible at others.

Takeaway: The Eagles' record is perfect, but their play is anything but.

There are no moral victories in the NFL, so you'd much rather be 2-0 and playing bad than 0-2 with two heartbreaking losses despite great play. That said, I'm not sure how Eagles fans can feel great about this team right now. They barely scraped by the Commanders in Week 1 and then needed a last-second touchdown to avoid an upset against one of the worst teams in the NFL. The inconsistency that haunted the team last year is still present, and the Cowboys and Giants are both improved. The NFC East is no longer theirs to lose.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Takeaway: The Bucs might just be bad.

Losing to Cincinnati in Week 1 wasn't exactly shame-inducing, but a home loss to the Cleveland Browns is exactly that. Tampa's defense made Deshaun Watson look like a competent NFL quarterback for the first time in like 5 years and the offense really couldn't do much. They might have entered the season as NFC South favorites, but it's clear right now that both the Saints and Panthers are better teams.

Takeaway: The Dolphins are the worst team in the NFL.

This won't come as much of a surprise to anyone who follows the league, but yeah, the Dolphins are terrible. The good news is that they are tanking properly and an 0-17 season isn't out of the question. The two other teams that could have staked a claim as the league's worst, the Titans and Browns, both showed up in Week 2 (and the Browns even won). Not only did the Dolphins lose, but they were run out of the building. They might be a historically bad team by the time the season ends.

Takeaway: Sean Payton is still overrated.

To be honest, I don't have much to say about this game. So, I decided to just remind everyone of my hottest NFL take. Sean Payton is a good NFL coach and he's treated like an elite one. He isn't, and the Broncos aren't that good. They'll be exposed in the next two weeks against the Rams and 49ers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Takeaway: The Chargers' season is over.

This might seem extreme, but I don't think it is. The Chargers have now lost games against the Cardinals and Raiders, not exactly world-beaters. Now, look at their upcoming schedule: at Buffalo, at Seattle, Denver, at Kansas City, at Los Angeles Rams, Houston, at Baltimore. It's possible the Chargers are going to be underdogs in each of their next seven games. I don't know how they recover at this point.

Takeaway: The Seahawks defense is very much the league's best.

There was a debate last year over whether it was the Seahawks or Broncos that featured the league's top unit but there's no such argument so far this year. Seattle held New England to 10 points in Week 1 and came up with a game-winning interception of Drake Maye. The Cardinals put up nearly 400 yards in Week 1 against the Chargers only to have the Seahawks hold them to 151 yards in Week 2. The NFC West is so stacked it almost seems unfair.

Takeaway: Injuries stink.

I was excited to see Jayden Daniels bounce back from an injury-plagued 2025 and return to his 2024 Rookie of the Year form. Then, right at the end of the first half, Daniels suffered another elbow injury and likely faces a lengthy absence. That stinks. For Dallas, it was a good response to the egg they laid in Week 1 against the Giants but the Daniels injury makes it hard to draw too many conclusions from this victory.

Takeaway: Is it possible for both teams to be happy?

Yes, the Colts lost and are now 0-2. Yes, I wrote earlier that teams would much rather be 2-0 playing poorly than 0-2 and playing well. But after getting blown out of their own building in Week 1 by the Ravens, this was a major step forward. And the good news is the Colts face the Texans, Commanders, Steelers, Titans and Vikings in their next 5 games, and all five of those games are winnable. For the Chiefs, what is there to say? They look great and poised to make another run at a Super Bowl.

item.title: Flying taxis are taking off in Texas. Is your city next?
item.description: Joby Aviation flew its eVTOL air taxi into DFW Airport's busy airspace as Texas launches Project Nexus, a three-year advanced air mobility program.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever watched your arrival time creep later while sitting in traffic, flying over it sounds pretty appealing. Texas is now testing what that could look like. Earlier this month, the Texas Department of Transportation launched the first phase of Project Nexus, a three-year program focused on preparing next-generation aircraft for use in Texas skies.

The Sept. 10 kickoff at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport included demonstrations from BETA Technologies and Joby Aviation. Joby brought its electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as an eVTOL. No passengers climbed aboard the initial Project Nexus flights. Instead, Texas is starting to learn how air taxis could eventually fit into the way people get around.

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, Sept. 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.

AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE

Project Nexus will advance in phases over the next three years. The broader first phase uses traditional aircraft, including helicopters and fixed-wing planes, to test routes and collect data. TxDOT says those initial flights will help validate routes and prepare for future advanced air mobility operations. Joby also launched a week-long campaign of piloted electric air taxi flights across North Texas under TxDOT's Project Nexus proposal, part of the federal eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The campaign included planned direct flights into DFW International Airport, a round trip to Arlington and a route connecting Alliance Airport with Toyota Motor North America's headquarters in Plano. One of the biggest tests involved DFW. Joby's campaign called for a direct flight into DFW's controlled airspace, with the aircraft landing at DFW Corporate Aviation. That puts an eVTOL into the same busy airspace used by one of the world's busiest airports. That kind of testing can tell regulators much more about how these aircraft might eventually operate around major transportation hubs.

We have been following electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as eVTOLs, for years. They can rise vertically like a helicopter. Many designs then transition into forward flight using wings. Earlier this year, we looked at how a federal pilot program could bring air taxis into U.S. skies before the industry reaches full commercial service. We have also covered plans for air taxis serving New York City's three major airports and Joby's partnership with Virgin Atlantic to develop electric air taxi service in the United Kingdom. So the aircraft themselves are no longer the biggest surprise. What gets my attention now is where companies are flying them and how regulators are testing their ability to operate around airports people already use. That's where Project Nexus comes in.

Flying around Dallas-Fort Worth creates challenges you do not get at an isolated test site. Joby's campaign included planned missions between Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport and several destinations around the region. DFW International Airport was part of that schedule. The company and federal researchers have been preparing for this type of operation for years. Joby says the FAA and NASA began studying electric air taxi integration in North Texas in 2018. Then, in 2023, Joby and NASA ran a detailed simulation examining whether the DFW terminal area could handle as many as 50 electric air taxi operations per hour. Now that work is moving from computer simulations to aircraft operating in North Texas. Joby has also leased a 45,000-square-foot facility at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport. The new facility gives Joby a long-term operating presence in North Texas, well beyond this initial flight campaign.

AI AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM PROMISES FEWER FLIGHT DELAYS

Here's where the Texas plan gets especially interesting. Air taxis tend to grab attention because people imagine hopping aboard and flying over traffic. But some early Project Nexus missions could have nothing to do with your commute. Later phases are expected to focus on medical and cargo logistics. TxDOT specifically points to transporting critical medical supplies or organs between rural facilities and urban medical centers in Austin and San Antonio. That's a use case that could be easier to understand than flying across town to save a few minutes. Moving time-sensitive medical supplies faster could show where this technology provides practical value while passenger operations continue developing.

Eventually, Project Nexus plans to put passengers onboard. TxDOT says the final phase will involve passenger air taxi flights across the Texas Triangle. TxDOT's plan calls for regional air taxi connections involving Dallas, Austin, San Antonio and Houston. That does not mean commercial passenger service across Texas has a firm launch date. Joby still has certification work ahead. The company says it has advanced into the fifth and final stage of FAA type certification, with testing continuing as part of that process. So you probably will not see an air taxi button appear beside your rideshare options tomorrow. The work happening now is about figuring out how these aircraft could operate safely before passenger service expands.

Texas is getting a lot of attention right now, but Project Nexus is part of a much larger federal effort. The eVTOL Integration Pilot Program includes eight projects across 26 states, with testing focused on passenger travel, cargo and medical transportation. We have already seen some of that play out. Earlier this month, we covered the FAA's testing of Elroy Air's pilotless hybrid-electric Chaparral cargo aircraft. BETA Technologies and United Therapeutics have also tested electric aircraft for transporting organs between Virginia and Maryland. Other projects involve New York and New Jersey, Florida and several additional states. So while Texas is one of the biggest air taxi test beds right now, it is far from the only one. That raises the bigger question: If these trials keep expanding, how long will it be before you start seeing aircraft like these closer to home?

DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES

If air taxis eventually come to your area, the big question will be simple: Will they actually make your life easier? Skipping over traffic sounds great, especially on the way to an airport or across a crowded metro area. But the convenience depends on where these aircraft take off and land, how much a ride costs and how much time you really save from door to door. You will also want to know what frequent flights sound like overhead. Electric aircraft are designed to be quieter than helicopters, but there is a big difference between hearing one occasionally and having them fly regularly near your neighborhood. And before any of this becomes routine, the FAA has to be comfortable with the safety side. That's exactly why these Texas tests are important. They give regulators a chance to see how the aircraft handle busy airspace before passenger flights become more common. For me, that is what makes Project Nexus worth watching. We already know these aircraft can fly. Now we are starting to find out whether they can fit into the way we actually travel.

I have been watching air taxis develop for years, but Project Nexus feels like the kind of test that can tell us whether they have a real shot at becoming useful transportation. Flying around North Texas and operating at DFW gives Joby a chance to show how these aircraft can handle the kind of busy airspace they would face in regular service. I am also really interested in the medical side. If an electric aircraft can move an organ or critical supplies faster between hospitals, that could be one of the first places where this technology shows its value. For passengers, though, I still come back to two things: price and convenience. If the landing site is 30 minutes out of your way or the fare costs a fortune, flying over traffic starts to lose some of its appeal. Noise will also be something communities pay close attention to as more of these aircraft take to the sky. We already know air taxis can fly. What I want to see now is whether they can save you enough time, at a price you can live with, to make you actually want to book one.

If an air taxi could turn an hour in traffic into a 15-minute flight, how much would you be willing to pay to take it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
