item.title: China ‘wiretapped Red Sea’ with spy hub 6 miles from US base: ex Pentagon official warns
item.description: China's upgraded base near Camp Lemonnier features new antennas and signals intelligence assets turning the Red Sea into a surveillance hub.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa.

The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications.

The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny.

"What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy, former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration.

CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES

"Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS."

The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset.

CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region.

The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said.

CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

"This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one."

"But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned.

"Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added.

Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters.

CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE

"The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said.

"I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said.

President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them."

Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan.

"They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters.

RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER

Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike."

"It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can."

The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces.

"We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained.

"Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth."

WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA

During the 2018 incident, the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries.

While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases.

"China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said.

"So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there."

IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS?

"It's our only base on the continent of Africa," he said, noting that it shares a "parking lot" with Japanese and Italian bases.

"At $66 million a year, it's the best money Americans spend on our defense budget, full stop."

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a choke point for nearly 16% of global maritime trade and, with significant crude shipments, Houthi attacks and pipeline disruptions have fueled a regional military buildup.

"Interference by China is in their strategic interest. They don't want to see the United States able to control their oil supply," Murphy said.

"China is far more reliant on Middle Eastern oil than the United States. China imports a huge portion — around 33% or more — of their daily oil needs and is highly reliant on long sea lines. You are seeing this muscle-flexing because they are far more reliant on Middle Eastern oil than we are."

TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

"Having intelligence is one thing, but you must have the ability to act on it. You need assets in the region," Murphy said.

"China doesn't have major combat assets outside their region because they lack a blue-water navy to project power outside the first island chain yet.

"That is coming, and they are working towards it quickly. Americans can take comfort in the fact that they don't have that capacity today, but we must stay alert because the only thing that subdues a threat is a ready posture," he concluded.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Chinese Embassy for comment.

item.title: Pickle-flavored snacks boom as sales jump 30% and craze hits new extremes
item.description: Gen Z's social media obsession is fueling pickle mania, from pickle pizza to fried pickle tacos, generating over 80 million engagements in 12 months.
item.content:encoded:
America's snack aisle is in a pickle.

From chips and crackers to nuts, popcorn and pretzels, pickle flavor is popping up just about everywhere.

Pickle-flavored snacks grew 30% in sales over the past year, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing data from market research firm Circana.

GEN Z TURNS ON CLASSIC SNACKS, FORCING MAJOR GROCERY SHAKE-UP: 'THEY DON'T TRUST THEM'

Beyond snacks, pickle flavor has expanded to smoothies, cheese spreads, hummus — even pickle toothpaste — and it's just getting started, a food and beverage trend expert told Fox News Digital.

"According to Datassential's Menu Trends platform, pickles appear on 46% of U.S. restaurant menus, growing 6% over the past four years," said Renee Lee Wege, trendologist and senior publications manager at market research firm Datassential.

"That doesn't seem like a lot, but for something already ubiquitous like pickles, that's notable, as it gets into formats like pickle pizza, pickle beverages, etc.," she told Fox News Digital. "We also predict an additional 5% growth on menus in the next four years."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Traditional pickles are most popular among millennials, but younger generations are driving the quirkier flavor applications, Datassential data shows.

Forty-eight percent of millennials love pickles, while 76% of this demographic loves or likes them. Gen Z trails in fourth place behind Gen X and boomers, though Wege noted, "that is pickle in general, which is tried-and-true, but pickle-flavored items, especially if they are unique or out there, would likely not be as appealing to older generations."

"Where Gen Z plays in is with the unique pickle-flavored items and creations that have been trending on social media, and we all know Gen Z's love affair with social media," she said.

Pickle flavor is being propelled by social media virality, Wege noted.

"From our social listening data, we see that pickles and pickle-flavored items generated more than 80,880,000 social-media engagements over the past 12 months," she said. "And recent chain examples include Smoothie King's Grillo's Pickles Smoothie, Del Taco's Fried Pickle Taco and McDonald's Dill Pickle McShaker Fries."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Pickle dip is another buzzy social media item, and coming soon to a pizzeria near you: pickle pizza.

"In Datassential's 2026 pizza trend data, pickle-related toppings are among the fastest-growing vegetable ingredients on pizza menus, with dill pickle up 73% and pickle up 46% over four years, indicating meaningful recent momentum for pickle pizza components," Wege said.

Pickles are ubiquitous and appeal to most consumers, Wege said, but what makes the current craze so pronounced is social media's ability to stir a frenzy around limited-edition offerings, combined with other trends.

"This is an evolution of 'maxxing' and consumers, particularly younger ones, looking for 'more is more' and maximalism," she said.

"Recent social listening data shows consumers are highly motivated by stronger, more distinctive flavor, with commentary around cane sugar emphasizing enhanced taste and flavor; this helps explain why bold, tangy pickle flavor resonates in the current environment."

Has America reached peak pickle?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Right now, I think we're in the upper echelon of pickle-mania," Wege said, "where the draw is more to 'what else could it do?' or 'make it even crazier and more jaw-dropping,' where the intent is to keep going bigger and weirder and more unique to get attention on social media and make it so consumers have no choice but to try it."

item.title: Attorney busts ‘biggest misconception’ in Karmelo Anthony filing that could be key in track meet murder case
item.description: Karmelo Anthony's 75-page filing of alleged threats, gun photos and violent texts may never have reached jurors, a Texas defense attorney says.
item.content:encoded:
A 75-page court filing detailing alleged threats, gun photos and violent text messages tied to convicted Texas killer Karmelo Anthony appears at first glance to be a roadmap of evidence prosecutors planned to present at trial.

But a veteran Texas criminal defense attorney says one of the biggest misconceptions surrounding the document is that jurors were never guaranteed to see any of it.

Fox News Digital recently obtained the filing, which prosecutors submitted before Anthony's murder trial under Texas Rule of Evidence 404(b).

UNTAPPED KARMELO ANTHONY EVIDENCE CACHE SHOWED HE STALKED EX-GIRLFRIEND, HAD 'KNIVES' OBSESSION: PROSECUTORS

The filing has taken on renewed importance because Anthony's bid for a new trial focuses on an alleged pretrial agreement governing character evidence. Anthony argues confusion over that agreement affected his decision not to testify, while prosecutors dispute that claim.

The notice catalogs dozens of alleged prior acts prosecutors said they may seek to introduce, including allegations that Anthony stalked his girlfriend hours before fatally stabbing 17-year-old Austin Metcalf at a Frisco high school track meet on April 2, 2025.

Prosecutors also cited text messages in which Anthony allegedly said he was "on the verge," posed with firearms, made violent threats and repeatedly discussed fighting.

KARMELO ANTHONY PHOTOGRAPHED WITH GUNS AS DOCS REVEAL ALLEGED HISTORY OF RAGE, THREATS AND VIOLENCE

The filing also includes allegations that Anthony talked about committing robberies, buying firearms and extended magazines, selling narcotics and threatening multiple people, including his then-girlfriend, in text messages spanning several years. Prosecutors also cited screenshots they said represent only portions of larger conversations and noted the alleged prior acts were separate from the charged offense.

To some readers, the filing might appear to be a blueprint of the prosecution's case.

KARMELO ANTHONY DEFENSE RESTS, ATTORNEYS PREP FOR CLOSING ARGUMENTS BEFORE JURY DELIBERATES IN MURDER TRIAL

But appearances can be misleading.

Tiffany Burks, a partner at Texas law firm Varghese Summersett and a former prosecutor, said that's not how Rule 404(b) works.

TEXAS JUDGE WHO PRESIDED OVER KARMELO ANTHONY MURDER TRIAL REMOVED FROM CASE OVER 'GOT IT RIGHT' COMMENT

Burks explained that filing a Rule 404(b) notice does not mean jurors will ultimately hear the evidence. Instead, it gives the defense advance notice of evidence prosecutors may seek to introduce, so attorneys have time to investigate the allegations and prepare a response before trial.

KARMELO ANTHONY BLASTS JUDGE IN NEW FILING OVER HANDLING OF MURDER TRIAL

If prosecutors believe they may want to introduce evidence of prior alleged bad acts, they must notify the defense before trial, so attorneys have an opportunity to investigate the allegations, prepare a response and avoid being surprised before a jury.

"The law requires that you file a 404(b) notice so that you can give the other side notice of what it is you may want to put in trial because the parties have to be prepared," Burks said. "Specifically, the defense has to be prepared to respond or rebut that information."

KARMELO ANTHONY ISOLATED IN JAIL AS TRACK MEET KILLER APPEALS CONVICTION, PREPS FOR PRISON STINT

In effect, the filing functioned as a placeholder, preserving prosecutors' ability to ask the judge to admit the evidence later if they believed it became relevant during trial. Filing the notice did not mean the judge would allow jurors to hear it, nor did it mean prosecutors would ultimately decide to offer every allegation listed in the document.

That also helps explain why Anthony's filing stretched to 75 pages.

CONVICTED KILLER KARMELO ANTHONY SENTENCED TO 35 YEARS AFTER YEARLONG LEGAL BATTLE: TIMELINE

Rule 404(b) generally prohibits prosecutors from introducing prior acts simply to argue a defendant has a bad character. But judges may admit that evidence for other purposes if it satisfies the rules of evidence.

"When I was a prosecutor, I would put everything but the kitchen sink in the notice," Burks said. "If you don't give the other side notice of it, then you're not going to be able to utilize it later."

AUSTIN METCALF'S FATHER HAUNTED BY KARMELO ANTHONY TRIAL VISUALS RELEASED: ‘I HAD NEVER SEEN THOSE PICTURES’

The filing reaches back to Anthony's school years in Louisiana and includes allegations of repeated fights, school suspensions, threats, assaults and misconduct. It also cites text messages in which Anthony allegedly wrote, "When I get mad i see red," "When I get mad i blackout" and "When I get mad i cant control myself."

After reviewing the filing following the trial, Metcalf's father, Jeff Metcalf, said he had "no idea" many of the allegations existed until he read the 75-page notice. Speaking with Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno, Metcalf said he was surprised by the scope of the filing.

Prosecutors also included photographs and videos they said showed Anthony with what appeared to be firearms, along with messages discussing shootings, robberies and narcotics.

The notice itself, however, is not evidence that those alleged acts occurred.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Instead, prosecutors identified them as evidence they said they might ask the court to admit at trial. The filing also cautions that some of the screenshots reflect only portions of larger text conversations.

Burks said prior alleged conduct can become especially important when a defendant argues self-defense because prosecutors often try to show the defendant – not the alleged victim – was actually the first aggressor. Rather than trying to prove someone has a violent character, prosecutors may argue prior conduct helps explain who started the confrontation, intent or another issue permitted under Rule 404(b).

"The prosecution can file a 404(b) notice to provide some information that can show that the defendant was, in fact, the first aggressor in the situation by showing information of previous aggressive acts," Burks said. "They can also use it to rebut a defensive theory."

Anthony argued he acted in self-defense when he fatally stabbed Metcalf during an altercation at a Frisco track meet. Prosecutors filed the 404(b) notice roughly a month before trial, preserving the ability to ask the judge to admit dozens of alleged prior acts if they later became relevant during trial.

The Collin County jury ultimately rejected Anthony's self-defense claim. Instead, the jury convicted him of murder and sentenced him to 35 years in prison after hearing testimony from more than 20 witnesses and reviewing surveillance video from the track meet.

SEND US A TIP

Whether jurors ultimately hear that evidence, Burks said, is a separate question.

GOT A TIP?

A judge must first decide whether each item is admissible under the rules of evidence before it can be presented in court.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Burks said many people mistakenly assume a lengthy Rule 404(b) filing means every allegation inside it will eventually be placed before a jury.

"I think probably the biggest misconception people have about 404(b) is they think that because you've given the other side notice of it, that it's automatically going to come in," Burks said. "That is not what it means."

Whether jurors ever hear prior-act evidence depends on what prosecutors ultimately seek to introduce and what the judge decides to admit.

item.title: Prince William refuses to repeat King Charles’ jealousy as Kate Middleton captivates royal crowds: experts
item.description: Prince William is "smitten" and "enchanted" by Kate Middleton after over a decade of marriage and three children, say royal experts to Fox.
item.content:encoded:
Kate Middleton has landed on her feet as the monarchy's brightest star, and Prince William is clearly enjoying the view.

"It's not just about duty," British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. "Prince William is not only proud, but he is smitten. He watches Princess Catherine and lights up. After more than a decade of marriage and three children, he is still completely enchanted by her."

"Few marriages have deepened in public admiration the way theirs has," Chard said. "They have achieved something very difficult — they have carved out a private life that works, and a public life that works. That balance is a great success."

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON ARE READY TO LEAD THE MONARCHY, SOURCES SAY: 'THANK GOD THEY’VE GOT EACH OTHER'

Chard's comments came shortly after former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond told The Mirror that the Prince and Princess of Wales have emerged as a power couple for the royal family, with Kate as its crown jewel.

"William and Catherine definitely have the wow factor that Diana had — and which spawned Di-mania," Bond told the outlet. "People today are equally mesmerized by the new Princess of Wales, so tall, so elegant and so chatty, but William just seems to purr with pride that his wife is such a star."

Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," agreed.

WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON IS THE MONARCHY'S SECRET WEAPON: AUTHOR

"The British people adore Kate in the same way they adored Princess Diana, the daughter-in-law she never met," Andersen told Fox News Digital. "But rather than be jealous of his wife the way King Charles was jealous of Diana's popularity, William is more than content to let Kate shine. In fact, there are times when he is perfectly happy to bask in her reflected glory."

"Kate has been William's rock for a quarter-century, and vice versa," Andersen continued. "What they have is the real thing. And I think Kate's cancer battle gave them a whole new perspective on life and a renewed appreciation of each other. It's all well and good to be proper and stiff in that British way, but why go to such lengths to hide their deep affection for each other? The spontaneous hugs, the loving looks — why wouldn't William be bursting with pride?"

"Kate continues to prove she is the royal family's Mary Poppins — 'practically perfect in every way,'" Andersen added.

Bond told the Mirror that while William is "pretty dashing and gets his fair share of crowd worship," his reaction to Kate's popularity contrasts sharply with that of his parents.

During the king’s marriage to the late Princess of Wales, royal watchers and photographers would clamor just to get a glimpse of her. Reports over the years have said Charles struggled with the attention Diana received.

In her controversial 1995 "Panorama" interview, Diana recalled a royal tour in 1983, saying, "We'd be going round Australia, for instance, and all you could hear was, 'Oh, she's on the other side.'"

"Now, if you're a man like my husband, a proud man, you mind about that if you hear it every day for four weeks," Diana said. "And you feel low about it, instead of feeling happy and sharing it."

Diana said it caused "a lot of jealousy" and that "complicated situations arose because of that." Charles and Diana separated in 1992, and their divorce was finalized in 1996, a year before she died at age 36.

"Luckily, William doesn't seem to suffer the same jealousy that his father did when Diana was the darling of the crowds," Bond said.

Following Kate's May visit to Italy, William said he was "very, very proud" of her.

"Rather than Prince William being jealous, his delight regarding her success is palpable," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Part of his joy is no doubt due to her strengthening the monarchy rather than detracting from it. His admiration for her is visible via his adoring glances and his general ease with her popularity."

"They have a jolly competitive spirit due to their love of sports, but they are also totally united," Fordwich said. "It's brilliant, both for their marriage and for the future of the monarchy."

William and Kate first met as students at the University of St Andrews. They became friends before their romance blossomed. In 2007, the couple split, with William later saying, "It was very much trying to find our own way, and we were growing up." They got back together that same year, and William proposed in 2010. They married in 2011.

The Prince and Princess of Wales are parents to three children: Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis. William is heir to the throne.

"He doesn't just see a wife," Chard said. "He sees the perfect future queen. Someone who can live in relative privacy while being in the public eye, which is exactly what the monarchy needs to survive. They also genuinely still adore each other. It's not performed for cameras."

"The public held a torch for Diana as they do for Princess Catherine now," Chard said. "William is also loved, but together, they have something more powerful than individual star power. He knows how valuable she is."

Chard also said William wants his wife to shine and feel confident in her royal role.

"He loves the fact that she is loved," Chard said. "He is in awe. It reminds him, in the best way, of the love his late mother received from the public. When he watches a crowd reach for Catherine, he doesn't see a rival for attention. He sees the woman he loves being adored, and he adores her all the more for it."

Royal watchers told Fox News Digital that Kate has grown increasingly confident in her role as she supports the king. Charles has continued carrying out royal duties following his cancer diagnosis. Andersen said Kate will be ready when the time comes for her to take on a greater role.

"William and Kate are doing their very demanding jobs with a smile, and that is largely due to Kate's innate positivity," Andersen said. "It's not overstating things to say the Princess of Wales is a force of nature, and every day William is reminded of that."

item.title: Trump’s massive Greenland deal makes clear who controls the Arctic’s strategic future
item.description: President Donald Trump's Greenland deal blocks China from military bases and sensitive investments on the strategic Arctic island near the U.S.
item.content:encoded:
Call it a win-win for Denmark and President Donald Trump. "The United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America. Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval," he posted on Friday.

Trump’s Greenland deal is a move to freeze out China and protect America in the Western Hemisphere. In decades past, Americans could indulge our natural aversion to foreign policy and bask in economic prosperity and a Western Hemisphere free of major threats.

Then China’s President Xi Jinping started pouring money into Arctic nations when he took over in 2012. Greenland was a prime target. The Greenland Self-Governance Act of 2009 provided no real barrier to Chinese investment in critical infrastructure. By 2017, the amount of Chinese foreign direct investment totaled hundreds of millions of dollars — equating to roughly 11% of Greenland’s gross domestic product. By comparison, Chinese investment in Canada constituted only 2.4% of GDP. China also tried to expand its footprint in Greenland by bidding on construction contracts to expand its airports, a move Denmark ultimately blocked.

SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE

Times have changed. And Trump is on it.

Greenland is a "highly strategic parcel of land," as Trump phrased it. Back in January at Davos, he called Greenland an "enormous unsecured island" and a "core national security interest of the United States of America."

Looking down from your globe, you see the major land masses guarding America are Alaska, Canada and Greenland.

The U.S. Space Force base at Pituffik, 750 miles north of the Arctic Circle, hosts a powerful phased-array radar that is part of the upgraded early warning radar network used to detect ballistic missiles, watch orbit lanes, and track satellites. Russia fires a nuclear weapon from a submarine in the Arctic? It’s the job of Pituffik to spot it. They also run radars for space situation awareness, which includes tracking nasty new maneuvering Chinese spaceplanes and satellites. Other units provide remote tracking and command and control to U.S. and allied satellites.

Trump’s agreement ensures China cannot install installations in Greenland to threaten these vital missions. Ever.

Greenland is basic to American security. You can’t have it dominated by Chinese money.

ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW

The fact is that 25 years of globalization (dating from China’s accession to the WTO) left Beijing entrenched on every continent. China’s Belt and Road Initiative, the Polar Silk Road: by any name, China’s economic investments sought to shake America’s natural alliances and geographic advantages. Trump is trying to reset the chessboard.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Not everybody sees it that way. Who can forget the outcry last winter when Trump proposed simply purchasing Greenland? NATO nations got their knickers in a twist. Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom sent troops along to a joint exercise with Denmark to show resolve. Trump threatened to tariff them. You’d have thought the world was ending.

RUSSIA PULLED BACK FROM THE ARCTIC, FOR NOW. NATO MUST ACT BEFORE THOSE TROOPS RETURN

Of course, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called this one right from the start. "The European leaders will come around. And they will understand that they need to be under the U.S. security umbrella," Bessent told NBC News on Jan. 18.

So did NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, the canny former Dutch prime minister, who stepped in to cool tempers and keep negotiations on track within the NATO family.

TRUMP ENVOY WARNS CHINA'S POWER MOVE AT SEA IS THREAT 'WE CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE'

"For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it," Trump ballyhooed.

The Greenland deal clears out Chinese influence from what Trump sees as North American territory. He’s followed that course with Panama, where Secretary of State Marco Rubio got Panama to back away from deals with China, and of course, Venezuela.

Is Cuba next?

item.title: House GOP not done with ActBlue after bombshell internal memos raise foreign cash questions
item.description: House GOP investigators warn their ActBlue probe is far from over as new findings allege the platform green-lighted donations despite foreign red flags.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: House GOP investigators are warning that they are not done with ActBlue after a bombshell report fueled questions over whether the Democrat fundraising giant is accepting foreign cash and lying to Congress about it.

"Whether it’s allowing fraudsters to steal taxpayer dollars or accepting illegal foreign donations through ActBlue, Democrats have proven themselves to be the party of fraud. Our investigation into ActBlue is far from over. We expect more documents and testimony in the weeks ahead," House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital.

ActBlue is a massive platform for campaigns to raise money that's used by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, among others.

Republican lawmakers have long accused the company of having lax verification standards for donors, something ActBlue has said it actively improved since the start of the GOP's probe. But new findings, first reported by Fox News Digital, appear to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from.

FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT

But the company maintains it did nothing wrong and signaled in comments to Fox News Digital that it has no plans to return any donations raised in the report.

HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE

Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital on Friday, "ActBlue’s own admissions raise serious questions about its fraud prevention practices, including a so-called passport verification process that did not actually verify or check entries against any government database. All options are on the table to ensure we get to the bottom of what is going on at ActBlue."

And a spokesperson for Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and the House Judiciary Committee confirmed to Fox News Digital that the panel "will continue aggressive oversight of ActBlue, including additional depositions."

All three committees have been responsible for investigating the left-wing fundraising giant.

It's not clear how much those depositions will yield, however. The Judiciary Committee revealed through a series of transcripts on Thursday that all 10 ActBlue employees and board members who appeared for closed-door depositions invoked the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions.

That includes co-founder Matt DeBergalis, whose invocation was first reported by Fox News Digital.

ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones similarly opted to plead the Fifth during a public hearing.

The GOP report cited a letter by Wallace-Jones to Steil, which maintained that donations on the platform made by people with addresses outside the U.S. required a passport number for verification.

But the Republicans' report alleged that the verification "only ensures that the entered passport number contains a certain number of characters, not that it is a valid U.S. passport number," rendering it an essentially meaningless step.

TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS'

The report also included excerpts purporting to show ActBlue supervisors green-lighting donations despite "red flags," including a memo lauding a donation as a "great accept," but noting, "Donor sometimes has an IP in Hong Kong, but none of their other signals raise any eyebrows."

Another communication appears to show an ActBlue supervisor maintaining that a denied contribution "should have been accepted." The rest of the memo stated, "It is a foreign contribution, but the name/email match, the IP/billing match, a full address with the correct country code, and there were previously accepted and successful contributions."

"The donor uses an Arkansas state code, which isn’t great, but [the] system can be wonky with requiring state codes for foreign donors," the rest of the message stated.

ACTBLUE SUES TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON, ALLEGING POLITICAL RETALIATION OVER DEMOCRATS' FUNDRAISING

An ActBlue supervisor also allegedly said a contribution "set off a lot of" alarms, but argued the donor should be given the "benefit of the doubt."

Yet another appeared to show an ActBlue employee acknowledging that a donor using a Missouri billing address had "all signs point to this person being from Canada," but that X (then Twitter) was used to confirm their identity.

But despite the GOP's accusations, the report's evidence also appears to show ActBlue employees standing by the platform.

An email from ActBlue employees shows they believe the company to be "the target of bad-faith political attacks at the hands of ill-intentioned operators." ActBlue also previously told the committee "there is no evidence that foreign donations through online or small-dollar contributions are a problem in U.S. elections."

The communications excerpts were included in the report and not independently verified by Fox News Digital.

It's prompted a firestorm on the right, with House Republicans' campaign arm demanding that Democrats return donations made through ActBlue.

"House Democrats cannot claim ignorance while continuing to rely on a fundraising platform facing serious allegations. The [National Republican Congressional Committee] officially calls on every House Democrat to cut ties with ActBlue and return any illegal contributions funneled to their campaigns through the platform," spokesman Mike Marinella said.

But when asked if ActBlue would return any donations, the company pointed Fox News Digital back to its statement on the House GOP report.

"There’s nothing to see here. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on," ActBlue said.

"Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign. This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda."

item.title: World leaders descend on New York for UNGA — but who really has America’s ear?
item.description: Over 100 world leaders descend on the United Nations General Assembly as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine dominate the diplomatic agenda.
item.content:encoded:
UNITED NATIONS, NEW YORK — More than 100 presidents and prime ministers will descend on New York this week for one of the busiest gatherings on the diplomatic calendar, arriving at a United Nations confronting wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, economic pressure from disrupted energy markets and fresh questions about the institution’s ability to respond to an increasingly fractured world.

The U.N. expects 73 heads of state and 45 heads of government, alongside 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told reporters Friday. Member states have already submitted roughly 1,000 requests for bilateral meetings, while 168 events are scheduled during high-level week, according to Dujarric.

Asked Friday to characterize the atmosphere inside U.N. headquarters as the delegations prepare to arrive, Dujarric described it simply as "high stress."

INDIA'S MODI-IRAN MEETING COMES AMID US WARNINGS OF SANCTIONS ON TEHRAN'S TRADING PARTNERS

The General Debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly begins Tuesday, Sept. 22, under the theme, "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all."

But beneath the speeches, motorcades and closed-door meetings across Manhattan is another competition: nearly every government represented in New York will be trying, in one way or another, to capture the attention of the United States.

"This is their moment to grab a piece of American mindshare for sure," Frank Ahrens, head of BGR Analytics, told Fox News Digital.

A new analysis released ahead of UNGA attempts to measure which countries already have it.

The 2026 BGR Impact Index, produced by BGR Analytics, the data practice of Washington-based BGR Group, ranks 197 countries and economies according to their overall footprint in the United States, combining economic, cultural, diplomatic, institutional and geopolitical measures. Japan holds the top position for a third consecutive year, followed by Germany, Canada, the United Kingdom and South Korea.

That competition is especially consequential this year.

TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS

President Donald Trump will return to the General Assembly on Tuesday with the US-Iran war entering its seventh month, while fighting involving the Iran-backed Houthis has placed new pressure on shipping through the Red Sea and raised fresh concerns among Gulf states about regional security. Reuters reported Sept. 18 that European and Asian allies have largely resisted U.S. calls to become more directly involved in the Iran conflict and that the prolonged war has strained Washington’s relationships with some partners.

The stakes extend well beyond Iran. The General Assembly agenda is expected to be dominated also by Russia’s war against Ukraine, Israeli-Palestinian tensions, Sudan, climate change and artificial intelligence. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov are among the prominent leaders or representatives expected to speak.

That combination of military power, diplomatic access and public perception gets at the central question behind BGR’s index: what does influence actually mean?

BGR compiled more than 100 indicators, ranging from GDP, population and foreign investment to international students, cultural presence and lobbying activity in Washington.

But one of the most consequential variables in this year’s analysis came from a much newer arena: social media.

"We looked at 4.9 trillion pieces of data across an entire year because we know that a social media campaign can really move a country's perception in the U.S.," Ahrens said. "And that was really the big takeaway from this year's index."

Social-media sentiment accounts for 20% of the index, second only to cultural imprint at 24%. Institutional ties and outward orientation each make up 16%, geopolitical nexus accounts for 10%, economic size 8% and lobbying and Washington influence 6%. BGR says its underlying data comes from publicly available sources, primarily the U.N., U.S. government agencies and established research institutions, while its social-media data is supplied by Meltwater.

For smaller countries, the analysis suggests reputation can produce particularly large swings.

Bahrain was the biggest riser, climbing 22 places, from No. 97 in 2024 to No. 75 in 2026. BGR attributed much of that increase to improved U.S.-facing online sentiment and increased visibility tied to Bahrain’s election to a rotating U.N. Security Council seat, its Arabian Gulf Cup victory and a USS Nimitz port call.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM

Georgia moved in the opposite direction, falling 31 positions, from No. 73 to No. 104. BGR said its deteriorating U.S.-facing online sentiment coincided with political unrest and arrests of journalists and opposition leaders.

Ahrens acknowledged that generating attention is not the same as wielding political influence. "Countries that make a lot of noise about themselves do get on the radar, but to stay on the radar, you have to have real accomplishments."

The index attempts to address that distinction by combining sentiment with harder measures such as economic links, institutional rankings, lobbying expenditure and participation in international organizations.

Perhaps BGR’s most unusual example of how national perception can change did not come from a president, diplomat or lobbying operation.

It came from a German soccer fan.

BGR calls it the "Freddy Effect," after a German World Cup visitor whose enthusiastic posts about traveling through the United States went viral this summer.

Ahrens said BGR found that positive sentiment toward Germany increased 13% over roughly three weeks during Freddy’s rise online. BGR links a substantial part of that increase to the reaction generated by his posts, although the data does not independently establish that he alone caused the change.

"Can you recreate a Freddy? I don't know if you can reverse engineer him to that effect," Ahrens said. "But what it shows you is how authentic communication really breaks through on social media."

It is a lesson that may resonate with delegations arriving in New York this week, where hundreds of leaders will have only a few days to secure meetings, shape headlines and make their country’s case.

item.title: After 6 months of war, US must prepare for a future after Iran’s government falls
item.description: The IRGC, Mojtaba Khamenei and Masoud Pezeshkian compete for power as Iran's Islamic Republic fights for survival amid escalating war and sanctions.
item.content:encoded:
Six months into the war, the central question about Iran’s regime is no longer its missile arsenal, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) ability to menace the Strait of Hormuz, or how long the confrontation can endure. The deeper question is political and historical: Who governs Iran? Is it Mojtaba Khamenei, whose position at the apex of the system remains opaque; Masoud Pezeshkian, whose office of president was never designed to hold sovereign power; or the IRGC, which after decades of accumulating military, intelligence and economic authority may have become the state’s true center of gravity?

Iran increasingly resembles not a Shiite theocracy protected by soldiers, but a militarized dictatorship in which the notorious clerical establishment provides ideological cover for the men with guns.

The Shiite Republic or Islamic Caliphate of mullahs emerged from the bleak winter of 1979 promising salvation and delivering coercion. Khomeinism turned political Islam into state power and terrorism, proxy warfare and revolutionary expansion into instruments of foreign policy. For nearly half a century, Tehran built armed transnational terrorist networks abroad while suffocating political life at home.

IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY

Now, this outlaw regime that once dreamed of exporting its revolution is consumed by a more primitive instinct: survival. War serves that purpose. Under its shadow, dissent becomes treason, criticism becomes collaboration and repression becomes patriotism. Washington must reject the regime’s oldest deception: Iran is not the Islamic Republic, and the Islamic Republic has never been Iran.

That distinction matters as economic pressure intensifies. Operation Economic Outcast seeks to sever the financial lifelines sustaining the regime and the IRGC, but Iran’s economic deterioration predates this war and cannot be blamed on sanctions alone. Corruption, ideological adventurism, institutional decay and the diversion of national wealth toward repression and regional militancy have exacted their price.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

Economic pressure may accelerate the regime’s exhaustion, but the deeper crisis is political and psychological: the widening gulf between a society seeking a place in the modern world and a ruling establishment imprisoned by the fears and obsessions of 1979.

Another uprising therefore cannot be excluded. No one can predict when humiliation overcomes fear and private anger becomes public defiance; history rarely announces revolutions in advance. Iran is under immense pressure: grievances have accumulated, the regime’s legitimacy has eroded, and successive uprisings have not been erased because repression has quieted the streets. The regime has contained anger, but not the conditions that produced it. Silence should never be mistaken for consent.

IRAN PREFERS CONFLICT WITH US OVER PEACE TO SUPPRESS INTERNAL UPRISING, HUMAN RIGHTS ACTIVIST WARNS

Yet the collapse of dictatorship and the birth of democracy are different historical events. Between them lies the dangerous terrain of transition. Iran’s next political order must be chosen by Iranians at the ballot box, not manufactured in Washington, Jerusalem, Moscow or Beijing.

Nor does every opposition faction carry equal political weight or vision. In my assessment, Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi occupies a distinctive position through his national visibility and advocacy of secular government, territorial integrity and democratic transition. His role and Iran’s constitutional future — republic or constitutional monarchy — must be decided by Iranians. Regime change should restore a nation’s right to choose, not merely destroy an old order.

Nor would the Islamic Republic’s collapse automatically bury the ideologies that have poisoned Iranian politics for decades. Islamism, authoritarian Marxism, sectarianism and separatism would compete for the vacuum. Democracy requires citizenship above ideology, national belonging above faction and the state above revolutionary militias. Iran’s transition will be difficult because the Islamic Republic has spent decades destroying the institutions a peaceful transition would need.

Washington’s record deserves scrutiny. Successive administrations have oscillated between confrontation and the hope that another negotiation might alter the regime’s character. Diplomacy can prevent wars, but the illusion begins when a tactical bargain is mistaken for strategic transformation. Tehran has learned to negotiate in one room while applying pressure in another, speaking diplomacy while preserving asymmetric warfare. A regime’s method of survival should not be confused with a change in its nature.

IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING

Tehran may calculate that America’s political calendar will restrain Washington before the November midterms. But Nov. 3 cannot define American national security. Iran is neither a Republican nor a Democratic question: its covert networks, terrorist capabilities and asymmetric retaliation concern the country itself. A regime fighting for survival may become more dangerous as its options narrow. Negotiation may alter Tehran’s tactics, but asymmetric pressure and deniable violence have been tools of its statecraft for decades.

The deeper lesson reaches back to 1979. Washington misunderstood not only the revolutionaries seizing power but the institutional rupture they were about to impose on one of the Middle East’s oldest nations. It was more than an intelligence failure; it was a failure of political imagination.

TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS

Nearly half a century later, America should not again imagine only two futures — accommodation with the Islamic Republic or chaos after it. Serious statecraft should prepare for a third: political transition that preserves Iran’s territorial integrity, national identity and continuity as a unified state.

The growing security cooperation among the United States, Israel and Arab states belongs within that horizon. Saudi Arabia faces Iran-backed armed groups, including the Houthis, while Israel and Arab governments confront overlapping security threats. Deeper cooperation — and potentially broader normalization through the Abraham Accords — could build a regional order less vulnerable to proxy warfare and transnational militias.

US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS

Any regional strategy begins with understanding Iran itself. American and Israeli policymakers — and the intelligence communities that inform them — should distinguish democratic Iranian nationalism from Islamist, Marxist, sectarian and separatist movements offering different futures for the country.

Iran’s territorial integrity and credible democratic actors should be understood before transition begins, not after institutions collapse. History is unforgiving toward governments that prepare for yesterday’s crisis; the worst morning to search for reliable Iranian interlocutors is the morning after a dictatorship loses control.

China embodies the final contradiction. Foreign Minister Wang Yi calls for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and preventing the war from spreading into Yemen and the Red Sea. Beijing’s anxiety is understandable: Middle Eastern energy arteries are also arteries of the Chinese economy. Yet China cannot demand stability while maintaining close ties with Tehran and avoiding confrontation over conduct that undermines it. Beijing wants open shipping lanes without confronting the forces threatening them — a policy that manages symptoms while leaving the disease untouched.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Hormuz, the Houthis, Tehran’s terrorist proxy networks, sanctions and war are not separate crises. They are consequences of the revolutionary order born in 1979, when ideology became an instrument of domestic rule and foreign policy. For decades, the West has confronted those consequences without resolving the underlying strategic problem.

The question after six months of war, therefore, is not merely how it ends, but what begins afterward. Iran’s future belongs to Iranians, but serious statecraft requires contemplating a future beyond the Islamic Republic. For nearly half a century, the world has built its Iran policy around the regime’s presumed survival. Beneath it stands a far older nation seeking to reclaim its political future. America need not write that future. It should ensure that when history next knocks on Iran’s door, Washington is not once again the last to understand what has arrived.
